messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 28
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Social Media Manager
  trauma_type: Military
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Visual (Injuries): Visible injuries or wounds on others, Driving with Others: Driving with people, Auditory (Helicopter): Helicopter or aircraft sounds
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Uniform or Weapons: Military, police uniforms or weapons, Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction, Avoid Physical Stress: Situations that put my body under stress
  Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
  Memory: Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
  Negative Appraisals: Outsider: I am permanently an outsider now, Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Liam is a 28-year-old social media manager who left the Army several years ago and now works in an open-plan marketing office where much of the day is spent scanning video clips, tracking trends, and coordinating campaigns. During his deployment, the moment that has stayed with him in the most broken way happened during what had seemed like an ordinary convoy movement. He was riding in a vehicle with other soldiers when an explosion struck nearby. What he remembers is not a smooth sequence but jagged fragments: the metallic force of the blast, the sensation of being trapped in the vehicle with other bodies, flashes of visible wounds on the men around him, and the chopping aircraft sound overhead as helicopters came in. Large sections are missing. At times he is hit with the same terror and helplessness without any picture attached to it, only the emotional force arriving all at once. Other times the whole thing feels so extreme and disjointed that he struggles to believe it really happened to him, as if it belongs to someone else’s life.

In the months after returning home, specific cues in ordinary life began to carry the event back into the present. Seeing visible injuries on strangers—a cyclist with blood on his shin, a coworker showing stitches after a minor procedure—could make his body surge before he had even formed a thought. The sound of helicopters over the city stopped him in place. Riding in a car with someone else driving was especially potent; being a passenger gave him the same trapped feeling he had felt in the convoy. In those moments he became intensely physically reactive, his chest tightening and muscles bracing, and if someone touched him unexpectedly he jerked hard with alarm. At night he found it difficult to fall asleep because part of him felt he had to stay alert, as though letting his guard down would be dangerous.

Because these reminders brought back either disconnected pieces of the convoy attack or raw emotion with no image, Liam began organizing his life around not setting them off. He avoided military or police uniforms and any visible weapons, crossing streets to stay clear of officers or leaving places early if a uniformed person came in. He avoided strenuous physical activity because an elevated heart rate and bodily strain felt too close to the state he remembered from the attack. He also started rehearsing conversations before almost any interaction, wanting to control every exchange and avoid being caught off guard. The more he lived this way, the less his memory ever settled into something coherent; it stayed in fragments and surges rather than becoming a story he could place in the past.

His work has become one of the places where the pattern is most visible. As a social media manager, he cannot fully avoid images from the public world, and when injury footage appears unexpectedly on a feed he feels a jolt of recognition before he can scroll away. On days when news clips include aircraft audio or emergency scenes, he becomes guarded for hours, speaks only after silently scripting what he plans to say, and avoids riding with coworkers to lunch or client meetings. If someone claps him on the shoulder from behind, he reacts sharply enough that colleagues notice. Those incidents leave him feeling exposed and different, and he has come to believe that he is permanently changed for the worse. He compares himself harshly to other people, thinking someone else would not have ended up so shaken or so unable to handle simple things like car rides or casual contact.

Over time, those beliefs have made the world feel even narrower. Because he sees himself as damaged and fundamentally outside ordinary civilian life, uniforms, weapons, injuries, and even the sound of aircraft seem to stand out more quickly to him, as if his mind is always finding proof that he does not belong anywhere fully safe. The more vigilant he becomes—especially at night and in situations where he cannot control what happens—the more he relies on avoidance to get through the day, and the more his body reacts when reminders break through anyway. Avoiding rides with others, steering clear of physically stressful situations, and overpreparing every conversation have begun to strain his relationship; his partner experiences him as distant and tense, particularly when he refuses spontaneous plans or flinches from unexpected touch.

Liam sought help after a recent week in which several things collided: helicopter sounds over his neighborhood, an injured pedestrian outside his office, and a mandatory work trip that would have required sharing a car with coworkers. He found himself unable to sleep, increasingly on edge, and ashamed by how much effort it took just to appear normal at work. What frightens him most is the sense that this is who he is now—cut off from other people, permanently altered, always one reminder away from feeling trapped again. What he hopes, though he says it cautiously, is that the memories might stop arriving as disconnected force and that he might someday sit in a car beside someone he trusts without feeling his whole body prepare for catastrophe.
